title: A Face in the Crowd
description: “I blur things to make everything equally important and equally unimportant.” [1]

All photographs in this series are self-portraits shots with an old phone camera which works as a black box [2] whose limitations heavily shape both the visual and conceptual language of the work. In a sense, these images function as anti-portraits: the subject becomes visible only as it begins to disappear, showing the self as a force rather than a subject: “despite appearances, there is no longer a story to tell; the Figures are relieved of their representative role, and enter directly into relation with an order of celestial sensations.”. [3]
references: [2] Vilém Flusser, Towards a Philosophy of Photography, 1983, Reaktion Books, p. 27
[3] Gilles Deleuze, Francis Bacon: the Logic of Sensation, 1981, Continuum, p. 9

title: Alexythimia
description:
Alexithymia is the inability to recognize, understand, or describe emotions [1]. 
This series renders famous works of art unrecognizable, transforming cultural masterpieces into estranged images that resist identification, representing this idea.

For Guy Debord, under capitalism, "all that once was directly lived has become mere representation". When being degrades into appearing, we become separated from our own emotions: "the more [the spectator] contemplates the less he lives" [2].   We no longer feel emotions but perform them, consuming images of feeling rather than experiencing it concretely.

The work may be expanded through an installation recording viewers' reactions to prints from this series, testing whether the condition it represents (emotional estrangement and failed recognition) manifests in the encounter itself.
references: [2] Guy Debord, The Society of the Spectacle, 1967

title: For Now We See Through a Glass, Darkly
description: J. M. W. Turner’s insistence on blackness as an expressive force — “if I could find anything blacker than black, I’d use it” [1] — and film-maker Scott Barley’s understanding of darkness and underexposure as material rather than absence — “to bring a tactility to vision, to go beyond figuration [...] and to feel the liminality between light and darkness as its own subject” [2] —, as well as Bernd & Hilla Becher’s concept of Typologien [3], strongly shape how I approach natural and rural landscapes in this project.
references: [1] Philip Gilbert Hamerton, The life of J. M. W. Turner, R. A., 1879, p. 296.
[2] Scott Barley, Notes on Cinema, URL: https://scottbarley.com/Notes-on-Cinema
[3] Bernd & Hilla Becher, Typologien, 2023, Schirmer Mosel
